analysis.one_liner: Sets nationwide limits on product liability lawsuits, restricting punitive damages and who can be sued.
analysis.headline: Backed by 45 cosponsors and a majority of the Senate — 57-41 on the final procedural vote — the bill failed two 60-vote tests in June 1994 and never got an up-or-down vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the 50 states' different product-liability rules with one federal set. It would make it much harder to win punitive damages against companies — none at all for drugs and medical devices the FDA approved or aircraft the FAA certified, unless the company defrauded the agency. It would limit who can be sued (stores and distributors mostly off the hook unless they were careless or made their own promises), make each company pay only its own share of pain-and-suffering damages, set a two-year filing deadline, and end most lawsuits over business equipment more than 25 years old. It also adds some tools for injured people, like fee penalties for companies who refuse reasonable settlement offers and then lose bigger at trial.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of cars, machinery, appliances, drugs, and aircraft, plus liability insurers and large retailers. They face fewer lawsuits, smaller and harder-to-obtain punitive awards, shorter filing windows, and no longer risk paying the full pain-and-suffering judgment when other responsible parties cannot. Businesses selling in many states also gain one set of rules instead of 50.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufacturers, liability insurers, and large retailers

how_it_helps.text: Bars punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved drugs and medical devices and FAA-certified aircraft and parts, unless the company withheld or misrepresented required information to the agency or bribed an official.

Lets product sellers (distributors, retailers) off the hook unless the injured person proves the seller was careless, breached its own express warranty, or had a reasonable chance to inspect the product.

Makes each defendant pay only its own proportional share of noneconomic losses like pain and suffering, eliminating joint liability under which a company with money could be made to pay the full amount.
Bars most suits unless filed within two years of discovering the harm, and bars suits over business 'capital goods' more than 25 years after delivery.

Requires punitive damages to be proven by 'clear and convincing evidence' of conscious, flagrant indifference to safety, and allows a separate trial on punitive damages so juries deciding compensatory damages never hear that evidence.

Gives companies a complete defense when an injured person was intoxicated and more than 50 percent responsible, and reduces judgments for people who reject a company's settlement offer and do worse at trial.
Establishes one uniform federal rulebook in place of differing state laws, reducing legal uncertainty for companies that sell nationwide.

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed by defective products. They would recover less and less often: no punitive damages for many FDA-approved drugs and FAA-certified planes, no full pain-and-suffering recovery when a small-share defendant cannot pay, a two-year filing window, and offsets tied to insurance or benefits they already received.

drawbacks.text: Punitive damages would be available only for 'conscious, flagrant indifference to the safety' of others, proven by clear and convincing evidence — a much higher bar than ordinary negligence — and entirely barred for FDA-approved drugs, devices, and FAA-certified aircraft, the products whose failures can injure the most people.
Each defendant would pay only its proportional share of pain-and-suffering damages, so if the main wrongdoer is insolvent or judgment-proof, the injured person goes uncompensated for the remainder.
A two-year statute of limitations and a 25-year cutoff for business equipment would end some valid claims, particularly for harm that shows up slowly.

Some businesses and insurers argue state-by-state liability rules are unpredictable and costly, and a uniform federal standard has genuine value; this bill's critics never offered their own federal uniformity proposal to compare.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's real value is uniformity — one national rulebook instead of 50 — and it does include some claimant-friendly tools like penalties on companies who refuse reasonable settlement offers and lose bigger at trial. But its largest, most detailed provisions all narrow corporate exposure: near-elimination of punitive damages for FDA- and FAA-regulated products, seller immunity, several liability, short deadlines, and intoxication defenses. The costs fall on people least able to bear them — those already hurt by a defective product — while the gains accrue to a concentrated set of manufacturers and insurers. On balance, the draft's design serves industry interests far more than injured consumers.

outcome.mechanism: A majority of senators wanted the bill, but opponents talked long enough to defeat two 60-vote cloture motions — 54-44 and then 57-41 — so it never reached a simple up-or-down vote, and the 103rd Congress ended with it still sitting on the calendar.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Sen. Rockefeller with 45 cosponsors — 36 Republicans and 9 Democrats — on March 31, 1993, and referred to the Commerce Committee.
The Commerce Committee held hearings, ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and reported it in November 1993, though minority views were filed; it was placed on the Senate calendar.
The Senate sent it to the Judiciary Committee, which held hearings in March 1994 and was then discharged, returning the bill to the calendar in April 1994.
The Senate took the bill up in June 1994, and cloture was sought twice; the first failed 54-44 and the second 57-41, both short of the 60 votes needed to end debate.
The votes fell largely along party lines: on the first cloture motion, 37 of 44 Republicans voted yes while 37 of 56 Democrats voted no.
After the second failed cloture vote the bill was returned to the calendar, and the Congress ended without the Senate ever voting on the bill itself.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People injured by defective products, consumer advocates, and the plaintiffs' bar kept the existing state-law system, under which punitive damages for dangerous drugs, devices, and aircraft remain available and companies with deep pockets can still be made to pay. Manufacturers, drug makers, aircraft makers, and insurers did not get the federal limits they had sought — though they got nothing worse either, since no federal standard was set.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers and the plaintiffs' bar

sides.party_line_note: Republicans backed it overwhelmingly — 37 of 44 and 38 of 44 voted for cloture — while most Democrats opposed it, 37 and 35 of 56 voting no; a Democratic sponsor and 9 Democratic cosponsors made it bipartisan on paper but not on the floor.

industries.note: The bill caps their exposure to punitive damages, shortens filing deadlines, ends most suits over equipment after 25 years, and ends joint liability for pain-and-suffering awards. The savings come out of compensation owed to people their products injure.

No punitive damages at all for FDA-approved drugs and devices, unless the company defrauded the agency. FDA approval would become a shield against the harshest civil penalty even when a product harms patients.
Same protection for FAA-certified aircraft and components. Crash litigation — historically among the largest punitive awards — would lose that exposure.

They would be liable only for their own carelessness, their own express warranty, or failure to pass on warnings, rather than being sued alongside the manufacturer for any defective product they sold.
Lower and rarer punitive awards, shorter exposure windows, and expedited settlement procedures all reduce claim payouts.

Fewer viable cases, fee calculations capped at community-standard hourly rates, and penalties for rejecting company offers would shrink contingency-fee work. In this bill their financial interest runs alongside their clients' recoveries.
